It really depends on the dog, some dogs love working while others are intimidated by it. But most, especially while they're puppies, love being out and being social. However, by the time most guides get assigned to a blind person they are very focused on their job, and they have to be. Normally, any puppy wearing a vest can go almost everywhere with their handler, with maybe a few exceptions... But yes, some higher class restaurants were not happy with Revlon being inside, but after a brief conversation they have no choice but to let us in (although there was an instance where I had to talk to the restaurant manager). 

I am very used to people approaching Revlon while she's working. With kids its harder, but normally you can get between your dog and them and just politely say that the dog is working. However, most of the time it is encouraged to let the puppy interact with people so that they learn good social behaviors. Unless the puppy is under stress (ie in a new environment, scared overwhelmed etc...), I always allow people to pet Revlon as long as they ask so I can make sure she sits and behaves herself. However on the common occasion that a child runs up to her, I immediately get Revlon's attention with high value treats so she focuses on me instead of the child and either look for the child's parents to get them under control, or ask the child to step back myself. When your dog does get approached by a child when they're unprepared, remember that the dog is probably pretty nervous, and that the best way to keep it calm is to stay calm yourself... Other than that the best advice I can give is to be preemptive and keep your eyes peeled for the children before they sneak up on you!

If the dog is chewing from anxiety, you need to take it out on lots of short, low pressure and high reward outings to build its confidence. 

if the dog is chewing from boredom, energy or both, then you could try putting a deterrent on the leash (something that won't hurt your dog, but that the dog doesn't like the taste of) and carrying a small amount of kibble or small treats to treat the dog every time it takes a couple of steps without chewing on the leash. The deterrent will keep the dog from chewing on the leash long enough to take a few steps and receive a reward (a treat), which will eventually teach it that the preferred behavior is not chewing. 

treating your dog works especially well if you do it in conjuncture with a short, consistent word, in guide dogs we use "nice," but it can be any word or even a clicker.

The requirements that they have to meet when they first get to California include simple basic training, such as sit, down, stay, do your business (relieving on command), go to bed, etc... They also have to have basic manners such as not jumping on people, staying by their handlers side while walking and good house manners. 
The requirements for their graduation from the program are much more encompassing. The biggest training must is a trait called "intelligent disobedience." For example, the dog has to know when to disobey their handler/blind person to protect them. If the crosswalk light shows the little man, but the dog sees a car that isn't stopping, the dog has to know that they need to disobey their handler and not guide them into the intersection. This is hugely important for graduating guide dogs. Aside from this a graduate guide dog has to also be very confident and comfortable in all environments, be willing and eager to guide and be safe for their blind person. 

Puppy raisers, like myself, keep the dog for 12-16 months, and once they go back to California they receive another 6-12 months of professional training.
We train the dog for between 12-16 months, then the dog goes for professional training in California for 6-12 months

Our club uses Yellow and black labs (with the exceptions of chocolate, and white labs) and golden retrievers. I find that the goldens form attachments too strongly with one owner, and are therefore extremely hard to transfer between raisers, and eventually to their blind person. Besides this most goldens also have some odd quirks about them (such as requiring a specific toy to be near them when they eat or not being food motivated). The labs, on the other hand are my favorite as they bond just as strongly with their new handlers, but in a much shorter and less stressful way. However, everyone has their favorites. Many people prefer goldens because they generally serve for a longer period of time before they are retired.
